cards.text: Boils all over Egypt, and Pharaoh, king of Egypt, STILL won't listen. So the LORD sends Moses, Israel's leader, back again: get up early, stand before Pharaoh, and say it one more time. "Let My people go, so that they may worship Me." Another early morning for Moses. Friend, that man's alarm clock has to be TIRED of him.

cards.question: If Pharaoh says no, the LORD will send all His plagues against Pharaoh, his officials and his people. What does the LORD want Pharaoh to know?

answers.text: There is no one like the LORD in all the earth
Israel is stronger than the army of Egypt
Moses is the greatest prophet in the land

cards.text: Then the LORD tells Pharaoh something wild. By this time, He could have stretched out His hand and struck Pharaoh and his people with a plague to wipe them off the earth. Could have. Didn't. I had to sit down on my gold base for that one.

cards.question: So why hasn't He? The LORD says He raised Pharaoh up to display His power to him, so that His ___ might be proclaimed in all the earth.
The LORD tells Pharaoh that he has finally started letting Israel go.

cards.text: Then comes the warning: "Behold, at this time tomorrow I will rain down the worst hail that has ever fallen on Egypt, from the day it was founded until now." Not "grab a jacket." Not "maybe stay in." The WORST. In Egypt's WHOLE history.

cards.question: The LORD even gives Egypt a heads-up before the hail. What does He tell Pharaoh to give orders to do right now?

answers.text: Shelter the livestock and everything in the field
Send the livestock away to the land of Goshen
Gather the people and pray to the gods of Egypt

cards.question: The LORD warns that every man or beast left out in the field will die when the hail comes down.

cards.text: So the warning's out, and Pharaoh's officials have a choice to make. It's the weather app saying 100% chance of hail. Some folks grab the umbrella. Some folks say, "Eh, they ALWAYS say that."

cards.question: What do the officials who feared the word of the LORD do?

answers.text: Hurry their servants and livestock to shelter
Ask Moses to call off the hail
Move their families into Pharaoh's palace

cards.question: The officials who disregarded the word of the LORD left their servants and livestock in the ___.

cards.text: Then the LORD tells Moses to stretch out his hand toward heaven, so hail falls on all the land of Egypt: on man and beast and every plant of the field.

cards.question: Moses stretches out his staff toward heaven. Along with the hail, what else does the LORD send?

cards.text: The hail falls, and the lightning keeps flashing right through it. Nothing like it had ever been seen in all of Egypt since it became a nation. Friend, I spent YEARS in a junk drawer that slammed shut, and that made me jump. This? I'd be under the parchment paper.

cards.question: The hail struck down everything in Egypt's fields, but it left the trees standing.
The hail pounds the land of Egypt. But just like with the flies, there's one place where it doesn't hail at all. Where?

cards.text: Then Pharaoh summons Moses and Aaron, Moses's brother. "This time I have sinned," he says. This time. Just this ONE time. All those other times? Let's not bring those up.

cards.question: Pharaoh keeps going. What does he say about the LORD?
Pharaoh has had enough of God's thunder and hail. What does he ask Moses to do?

cards.text: Pharaoh even promises to let them go. Moses says that once he's left the city, he'll spread out his hands to the LORD, and the thunder and hail will stop.

cards.question: Moses says the storm will stop so that Pharaoh may know that the earth is the ___.
Moses tells Pharaoh he knows that Pharaoh and his officials finally fear the LORD.

cards.text: Now a quick note in the text about the crops. The flax and barley were destroyed, since the barley was ripe and the flax was in bloom. Timing is everything. Ask anybody who's ever pulled a batch out of the oven too early.

cards.question: The wheat and spelt were destroyed by the hail too.

cards.text: Moses leaves Pharaoh, goes out of the city and spreads out his hands to the LORD. The thunder and hail stop, and the rain no longer pours down on the land.

cards.question: The sky goes quiet, and Pharaoh sees the storm is over. What does he do?

answers.text: He sins again and hardens his heart
He lets the Israelites go at once
He sends Moses a gift of thanks

cards.question: Pharaoh hardened his heart, and so did his ___.

cards.text: So Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he wouldn't let the Israelites go, just as the LORD had said through Moses. Keep your apron on, friend. This story is a long way from done.

findings.problem: The opening card has five sentences: the setup, the sending, the quote, "Another early morning for Moses" and the alarm clock joke.

rule.text: The opening card can be up to 3 sentences. It says who is speaking, to whom, and what is going on.

findings.problem: The card states a fact from the previous passage (boils all over Egypt, and Pharaoh still won't listen, Exodus 9:8-12) without its reference. The card cites only Exodus 9:13.

rule.text: Facts from outside the passage are fine when they help, like who a new person is or who wrote a letter, with their reference.

findings.problem: This story card has five sentences: "Then the LORD tells Pharaoh something wild." / "By this time..." / "Could have." / "Didn't." / "I had to sit down..."

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: This story card has four sentences: the setup plus three sentences of the weather app joke.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: This story card has four sentences.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: The drawer joke doesn't click. A drawer that "slammed shut" and made him jump doesn't share the core action of a terrifying storm, so a stranger would say "huh?"

rule.text: If a stranger would say "huh?", rewrite it.

findings.problem: The drawer slamming shut is a new detail added to his backstory, which describes the drawer rattling and pulling open. Hiding "under the parchment paper" calls back to the bakery bin, a detail that hasn't been set up in this lesson.

rule.text: He can talk about them freely, but never adds anything new to them.

findings.problem: "Left the trees standing" is arguably true. Exodus 9:25 says the hail "stripped every tree." A stripped tree can still be standing, so a baker could argue for True.

rule.text: No near-matches. A wrong answer never means the same as the right answer, or close to it. If a baker could argue it's right, replace it.

findings.problem: "Just like with the flies" states a fact from an earlier passage (Goshen spared from the flies, Exodus 8:22) without its reference.

rule.text: Facts from outside the passage are fine when they help, like who a new person is or who wrote a letter, with their reference.

findings.problem: This story card has six sentences.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: This story card has four sentences.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: The comparison has a different action. The barley and flax were destroyed because they were ripe and in bloom, while the late crops were spared. "Pulled a batch out of the oven too early" is about being too early, which is the opposite situation.

rule.text: The everyday comparison must have the same action.

findings.problem: The last story card has three sentences: the verse plus a two-sentence story-continues line.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: Story cards 1, 9 and 14 are plain retellings with no trace of Papa Dorin's voice, at big moments: the hail called down, Pharaoh's promise and the storm stopping.

rule.text: Short, but not stripped down. A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.
